PA-28: PA-28 is a low-wing light aircraft with the wings mounted below the cabin rather than above it like a Cessna 172 or Cessna 208.
PA-28 has a single piston engine mounted in the nose.
PA-28 uses a two- or three-blade propeller at the front of the aircraft.
PA-28 has fixed tricycle landing gear with a simple light-aircraft stance.
PA-28 has a conventional tail with one vertical fin.
PA-28 has low-mounted horizontal stabilizers on the aft fuselage.
PA-28 has rectangular to slightly tapered wings with blunt tips.
PA-28 has a compact general aviation fuselage that is much shorter than the long utility fuselage of a Cessna 208.
PA-28 has a boxier cabin and fuselage shape than the rounder, more sculpted SR-20.
PA-28 has traditional side cabin windows instead of the more canopy-like cockpit glazing seen on an SR-20.
PA-28 has a simple rounded nose profile ahead of the propeller without the sleek, composite-style shaping of an SR-20.
PA-28 has a small 2- to 4-seat light-aircraft body rather than the larger cabin volume of a Cessna 208.
PA-28 has a low-slung profile on the ground because the fuselage sits beneath the wings.
PA-28 has a single-engine tractor layout rather than any wing-mounted engine arrangement.
PA-28 has a straight, unswept wing planform typical of a light piston aircraft.
PA-28 has a more angular rear fuselage and tailcone than the more bulbous SR-20.
PA-28 has a conventional metal light-aircraft appearance with a straightforward fuselage and tail layout.
PA-28 has a noticeably lower wing placement than the high-wing utility shape of a Cessna 208.
PA-28 has a narrower, less elongated fuselage than the larger high-wing Cessna singles in this group.
PA-28 has the classic Cherokee-family combination of a low wing, nose propeller, fixed tricycle gear, and conventional tail.
Tornado: Tornado has variable-sweep wings that may be fully spread or swept sharply back.
Tornado carries two jet engines buried in the rear fuselage with twin exhausts side by side.
Tornado has a single vertical tail fin rather than the twin tails of the F/A-18.
Tornado shows boxy side-mounted air intakes just behind the cockpit on both sides of the fuselage.
Tornado has a long pointed nose extending well ahead of the cockpit.
Tornado usually has a long two-seat canopy with a stretched cockpit section.
Tornado has shoulder-mounted wings that blend into a deep, slender fuselage.
Tornado carries low-mounted horizontal tailplanes on the rear fuselage below the fin.
Tornado has a deeper and heavier-looking fuselage than the lighter Hawk T1.
Tornado is less delta-like in planform than the Eurofighter Typhoon, especially with wings unswept.
Tornado has a longer, more substantial fuselage than the compact F-16A/B.
Tornado lacks the fixed wing shape of the Typhoon, F-16A/B, F/A-18, and Hawk T1 because its wings pivot.
Tornado has its main landing gear retracting into the fuselage area rather than into slim wing roots.
Tornado presents a broad rear fuselage to house its two closely spaced exhaust nozzles.
Tornado has wings mounted higher on the fuselage side than many low-wing fighter designs.
Tornado combines one fin with two exhausts, a layout that separates it from single-engine fighters like the F-16A/B and Hawk T1.
Tornado has engine intakes with a squarer, more rectangular appearance than the rounder style seen on some other fighters.
Tornado has a long continuous upper fuselage line from the canopy back to the fin.
Tornado appears as a medium-to-large strike fighter, bulkier than the Hawk T1 and F-16A/B.
Tornado has a distinctly swing-wing family silhouette with a pointed nose, deep fuselage, single fin, and twin rear exhausts.
Spitfire: Spitfire has a single nose-mounted piston engine with a propeller spinner.
Spitfire uses low-mounted wings with a broad elliptical shape and rounded tips.
Spitfire has much more rounded elliptical wings than the straight narrow wings of the DH-82 and DHC-1.
Spitfire has a slim streamlined fuselage with a long nose ahead of the cockpit.
Spitfire has a single-seat fighter canopy rather than the tandem open cockpits of the DH-82.
Spitfire has a conventional tail with one vertical fin and low horizontal stabilizers.
Spitfire is a taildragger with two main wheels under the wings and a small tailwheel.
Spitfire has main landing gear that retracts outward into the wings.
Spitfire lacks jet intakes and underwing engines because it is a propeller-driven fighter.
Spitfire is much smaller and more compact than the modern Hawk T1 and Eurofighter Typhoon jets.
Spitfire has a smoothly curved wing leading edge instead of the Eurofighter Typhoon's delta planform.
Spitfire has a pointed spinner nose rather than a blunt trainer nose.
Spitfire has only one engine, unlike twin-jet fighters with paired side intakes.
Spitfire has a sleek WWII fighter fuselage without the boxy open-cockpit structure of the DH-82.
Spitfire has wings set low on the fuselage rather than stacked biplane wings.
Spitfire has rounded wing tips that reinforce its classic elliptical wing outline.
Spitfire has a framed or bubble fighter canopy placed well aft of the engine cowling.
Spitfire has no tricycle landing gear, unlike the Hawk T1 and Eurofighter Typhoon.
Spitfire has a narrow rear fuselage that tapers cleanly toward the tail.
Spitfire has classic single-engine fighter proportions with one propeller at the nose and no jet exhaust arrangement.
MD-87: MD-87 has a noticeably shorter fuselage than the standard MD-80, giving it a compact stretched-DC-9 appearance.
MD-87 carries two turbofan engines mounted on the rear fuselage, one on each side.
MD-87 has no engines under the wings, so the low-mounted swept wings appear clean and unobstructed.
MD-87 uses a T-tail with the horizontal stabilizer mounted high on top of the fin.
MD-87 has a single vertical tail above a long rear fuselage engine installation.
MD-87 shows the classic MD-80 family pointed nose with a relatively small cockpit windshield area.
MD-87 is a narrow-body twinjet with a long slim body despite being shorter than other MD-80 variants.
MD-87 has low-mounted wings with moderate sweep set well below the cabin windows.
MD-87 retains the MD-80-style rear fuselage and tailcone, unlike the more modern-looking Boeing 717.
MD-87 has older-style rear engine nacelles rather than the Boeing 717's newer nacelle shape.
MD-87 appears much shorter overall than the MD-90 while keeping the same rear-engined family layout.
MD-87 has a more updated MD-80-family tailcone and aft-body shape than the earlier DC-9-30.
MD-87 keeps the classic rear-engined short-to-medium-haul jet proportions of the MD-80 family in a shortened body.
MD-87 has a conventional tricycle landing gear arrangement beneath a rear-engined narrow-body fuselage.
MD-87 presents a compact fuselage length combined with the same tall T-tail seen on longer MD-80 family members.
MD-87 has passenger doors positioned along a shortened narrow-body fuselage, with the aft section compressed compared with the MD-80.
MD-87 shows a slim cylindrical fuselage cross-section typical of the DC-9 and MD-80 lineage.
MD-87 has the main landing gear mounted under the wing-root area rather than in pods or fuselage sponsons.
MD-87 combines a short fuselage with rear-mounted turbofans, separating it from wing-engined narrow-body airliners.
MD-87 retains the family's classic pointed front end and long aft-mounted engine section despite its reduced overall length.
Tu-134: Tu-134 has two turbofan engines mounted on the rear fuselage, one on each side.
Tu-134 uses a T-tail with the horizontal stabilizer set high on the vertical fin.
Tu-134 has low-mounted swept wings attached well below the cabin windows.
Tu-134 has a slim, relatively short narrow-body fuselage with compact proportions.
Tu-134 shows a pointed, heavily glazed nose that gives it a bomber-like cockpit profile.
Tu-134 lacks underwing engines, leaving the wings visually clean compared with many twinjets.
Tu-134 has only two engines, unlike the three-engine Yak-42 and 727-200.
Tu-134 has a more extensively glazed nose than the DC-9-30 and MD-80.
Tu-134 has a shorter and less stretched fuselage than the MD-80.
Tu-134 appears smaller and more compact overall than the 727-200.
Tu-134 carries its main landing gear in prominent fairings near the wing root area.
Tu-134 has a rear fuselage that narrows cleanly toward the tail between the engine nacelles.
Tu-134 has engine nacelles mounted tight to the aft fuselage rather than on pylons under the wings.
Tu-134 has a classic early-jet appearance with a sharp nose and simple cylindrical body.
Tu-134 has a vertical fin rising above the rear-mounted engines to support the high tailplane.
Tu-134 has cabin windows running along a short, straight-sided fuselage segment between nose and tail.
Tu-134 has wings swept back more strongly than on many propeller airliners, reinforcing its jetliner profile.
Tu-134 has a noticeably pointed front fuselage instead of the blunter nose common on the DC-9 family.
Tu-134 has a compact tail-mounted twinjet layout without the center intake seen on trijets.
Tu-134 combines a glazed navigator-style nose, rear engines, and a T-tail in a distinctive Soviet-era airliner silhouette.
Tu-154: Tu-154 has three rear-mounted turbofan engines with the third engine fed by an intake at the base of the vertical tail.
Tu-154 uses a tall T-tail with the horizontal stabilizer mounted high on the fin.
Tu-154 has low-mounted swept wings that are more strongly swept than those of the Yak-42.
Tu-154 shows a long, slim narrow-body fuselage with straight rows of cabin windows.
Tu-154 has a single vertical tail that is taller and more prominent than the Yak-42 fin.
Tu-154 carries its two side engines on the rear fuselage rather than under the wings.
Tu-154 is a trijet, unlike the twin-engined DC-9-30 and MD-80.
Tu-154 has a bulkier and heavier-looking landing gear area than the Boeing 727-200.
Tu-154 shows prominent main landing gear fairings around the wing root and lower rear fuselage.
Tu-154 has a more substantial wing root structure than the 727-200.
Tu-154 presents a robust, heavy-set stance compared with the slimmer-looking 727-200.
Tu-154 has a longer and more airliner-like fuselage than the shorter Yak-42.
Tu-154 combines a narrow-body fuselage with three tail-mounted engines as a key family cue.
Tu-154 has a center engine intake blended into the fin root through an S-duct rather than a separate pod.
Tu-154 has a conventional pointed airliner nose with cockpit glazing set above the narrow fuselage.
Tu-154 has rear fuselage engine nacelles mounted close to the body on both sides.
Tu-154 has wings mounted low on the fuselage instead of shoulder-mounted or high-mounted.
Tu-154 shows a larger T-tail proportion relative to the fuselage than the Yak-42.
Tu-154 has a non-widebody cylindrical fuselage cross-section with multiple passenger windows in a straight line.
Tu-154 has a more complex and prominent lower fuselage landing gear fairing area than the 727-200.
Yak-42: Yak-42 is a trijet with two engines mounted on the rear fuselage and a third engine fed by a dorsal intake at the base of the fin.
Yak-42 has a T-tail with the horizontal stabilizer mounted high on the vertical tail.
Yak-42 has low-mounted swept wings attached below the fuselage.
Yak-42 has a slim narrow-body fuselage of medium length with compact, slightly stubby proportions.
Yak-42 has a pointed nose with a more modern, less heavily glazed cockpit area than the Tu-134.
Yak-42 is larger and longer-bodied than the Tu-134.
Yak-42 is shorter and stubbier in overall proportions than a Boeing 727-200.

Yak-42 carries its main landing gear under the wing root and fuselage area rather than on long rear-fuselage stalks.
Yak-42 has a broad, blended tail-root area where the dorsal intake merges into the fin.

Yak-42 has a cleaner wingtip shape without the prominent wingtip devices often seen on later airliners.
Yak-42 shows rear-mounted side engines set close to the aft fuselage on both sides.
Yak-42 has a less pronounced center-engine S-duct intake shape than the Boeing 727-200.
Yak-42 has a fuller rear fuselage and tail intake combination than the slimmer-lined Tu-134.
Yak-42 is a narrow-body airliner rather than a wide-body jet, with a single-aisle fuselage cross section.
Yak-42 has wings that appear more substantial and broader in chord than those of the smaller Tu-134.
Yak-42 has a vertical tail that rises directly above the dorsal engine intake, creating a tall central tail unit.
Yak-42 has a cockpit and nose profile that appears more rounded and contemporary than the sharper glazed nose style of older Soviet trijets.
Yak-42 has three visible jet exhaust positions at the rear, one central and two on the sides, unlike the two-exhaust DC-9 and MD-80 families.
